docs.title: BrainLabLLM
docs.text:
A desktop app that gives your lab a private AI chat and meeting-notes assistant — running entirely on lab hardware, with no cloud services involved.

  • AI Chat

    Chat with your lab's local language model. Attach code or text files for context, regenerate replies, copy responses, and keep a searchable history.

  • Meeting Transcription

    Record a meeting, get a full transcript from a locally-run speech-to-text model — no audio ever leaves your machine.

  • AI Summaries

    Turn any transcript into structured notes — Key Points, Decisions, Action Items — with one click, even for hour-long meetings.

  • Wiki & Web Lookup

    Opt-in, per-message tools that let the assistant fetch a page from the lab's internal wiki or search the public web to answer a specific question — both staying on the lab network.

  • AI Coding Agent

    An approval-gated assistant that can read, edit, and run commands in a project folder on your machine — every change is shown to you before it happens.

  • Zero-Friction Install

    A double-click installer. No Python, no command line, no accounts. Speech recognition works fully offline out of the box.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Cloud AI assistants are convenient, but sending meeting audio or proprietary code to a third-party service isn't always an option. This tool runs the two AI workloads it needs — speech-to-text and language generation — on infrastructure your lab already controls:

  • Speech-to-text runs locally on your own machine, via a bundled faster-whisper model. It works with no network connection at all.
  • Chat and summarization talk to a language model running on a shared lab server over your local network — nothing leaves the building.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
The app has three tabs:

Chat — a familiar chat interface with a conversation sidebar, markdown-formatted replies (including syntax-highlighted code blocks), file attachments, and opt-in wiki lookup / web search per message.

Meeting — pick a microphone, hit Record, talk. When you stop, the full recording is transcribed in one pass and shown in a transcript panel. From there, a Summarize button produces structured notes, and you can export or save the result.

Agent — point it at a project folder and ask for a code change; it proposes edits and commands, and nothing runs until you approve it.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: OS Windows 10 or 11 Network Lab network access, for chat and summarization only GPU Optional — speeds up transcription significantly, but the app runs fine on CPU Disk space ~2 GB (includes the bundled speech model) Technical skill None — see Installation

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page is for anyone maintaining, extending, or just curious about how the app is built. It documents not just what the system does, but why it's built this way — several design choices here came from things that didn't work in earlier iterations.

docs.title: System overview
docs.text:
Two AI workloads, running in two different places:

flowchart LR
    subgraph local["Your machine (fully offline)"]
        UI["Tkinter UI\n(main.py)"]
        MIC["Microphone"] --> REC["Audio capture\n(meeting.py)"]
        REC --> STT["faster-whisper\n(bundled, local)"]
        STT --> UI
    end

    subgraph lab["Lab network"]
        OLLAMA["Ollama server\n(qwen3.6-coder)"]
    end

    UI <--> |"chat + summarization\nHTTP, requires network"| OLLAMA

    style local fill:#EEEBFF,stroke:#6C5CE7
    style lab fill:#E4F9F3,stroke:#00B894

Speech-to-text never leaves the machine. Audio is captured, transcribed, and discarded locally — this is a deliberate privacy property, not an implementation detail. Only text (chat messages, transcripts being summarized) goes over the network, to the lab's own Ollama server.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text: File Responsibility main.py The Tkinter UI (ChatApp), configuration/settings persistence, chat networking (query_ollama_stream), and the map-reduce summarization logic. meeting.py Everything audio: device enumeration, recording (AudioRecorder), and the record-then-transcribe orchestrator (MeetingSession). No UI code and no dependency on main.py. theme.py Centralized color palette and ttk.Style configuration — the single source of truth for the app's visual design. agent.py The coding-agent tool-calling loop (AgentSession), its tools (read/list/search/write/edit/run-shell), and the path-scoping security boundary (resolve_scoped_path). No UI code and no dependency on main.py, same as meeting.py. diarization.py Speaker identification (diarize, assign_speakers_to_segments) — a separate model layered on top of, not replacing, meeting.py's transcription. No UI code and no dependency on main.py or meeting.py. wiki.py Lookup tool for the lab's internal MediaWiki (fetch_wiki_page). No UI code and no dependency on main.py. websearch.py Lookup tool for public web search via a local SearXNG instance (search_web). Same shape and independence as wiki.py — see Web search. installer.py A minimal, dependency-free Tkinter installer GUI, built separately from the main app (see Packaging).

docs.title: Why batch transcription, not live
docs.text:
An early version of the Meeting tab transcribed audio while recording, using a hand-rolled energy-threshold voice-activity detector (VAD) to chop continuous audio into utterances, transcribing each as it completed. This looked good in initial tests with clearly-paced, pause-separated speech.

Under real conditions — a person speaking quickly and continuously, the way people actually talk in meetings — it broke down in two specific ways:

  1. Fragmentation. Natural micro-pauses (a breath, a half-second hesitation) were frequently mistaken for sentence boundaries, splitting one continuous thought into two disconnected fragments.
  2. Hallucination. Very short, decontextualized audio clips are a known failure mode for Whisper-family models — with little context to work from, the model sometimes produced plausible-sounding but entirely fabricated text (a well-documented pattern; "Thank you for watching" on near-silent audio is a famous example of this class of error).

Tuning the VAD (longer silence thresholds, a debounce requiring sustained signal before committing to a segment, feeding the previous segment's text back in as context for the next) reduced but didn't eliminate the problem.

The fix was architectural, not a bigger tuning pass: record the entire meeting as one continuous buffer, and transcribe it once, using faster-whisper's own built-in VAD filtering (vad_filter=True, backed by Silero VAD internally) — which is more sophisticated than the hand-rolled version, and critically, has the entire recording's context available when deciding where sentence boundaries actually are, rather than making that call in real time from a small rolling window.

The trade-off is explicit: no incremental transcript while recording, in exchange for a transcript that's reliably coherent. For meeting notes, that's the right trade.

docs.title: Speaker diarization: GPU-only, layered on top
docs.text:
"Identify speakers" is a second, independent model (diarization.py, pyannote.audio) layered on top of faster-whisper's transcript, not a replacement for it — Whisper still does the actual speech-to-text; diarization only answers who was talking when, and the two results are merged afterward by overlapping their timestamps.

Model choice: pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1, not -3.1. The more commonly-referenced -3.1 pipeline additionally depends on a separately-gated pyannote/segmentation-3.0 model — two Hugging Face license acceptances instead of one. The community pipeline needs only itself, has better published accuracy, and ships under an explicit CC-BY-4.0 license. Fewer gated dependencies for whoever builds this app from source, for no accuracy cost — better on every axis that mattered here.

GPU-only, with no CPU fallback. Unlike Whisper transcription — which already has a proven, acceptable CPU path used throughout this app — real-world CPU performance for pyannote is genuinely unpredictable across unknown lab hardware; published benchmarks and real-world reports for this class of model disagree by an order of magnitude depending on hardware. Rather than risk a lab machine hanging for minutes on what looks like a hung app, the checkbox (meeting_identify_speakers_check in main.py) starts disabled and only enables once a background-thread check (diarization.gpu_available(), a lazy torch.cuda.is_available()) confirms a usable GPU exists. This mirrors the generation-token/root.after(0, ...) pattern described above: the check never blocks Meeting-tab construction.

The torchcodec workaround. pyannote's own file-path audio loading depends on torchcodec, which fails to load its native DLL in this environment (a PyTorch/torchcodec build mismatch, the same category of Windows DLL friction already documented in Packaging for other ML dependencies). Rather than chase that DLL, diarize() always feeds pyannote pre-decoded audio as a {"waveform": tensor, "sample_rate": ...} dict — reusing faster_whisper.audio.decode_audio(), a dependency this app already has a working relationship with, instead of adding a second audio-decoding path. This is pyannote's own documented workaround for the same issue, not a workaround invented for this app specifically.

Failure is graceful, not fatal. A transcription failure is a hard error (MeetingSession.on_error) — there's no usable output without it. A diarization failure is different: _transcribe_with_optional_diarization() catches any exception from the diarization step and falls back to the plain, unlabeled transcript, surfacing only a status message. Losing speaker labels on an otherwise-successful transcription shouldn't cost the user their meeting notes.

Segment-to-speaker alignment picks the best overlap, not the first match. assign_speakers_to_segments() compares each Whisper segment against every diarization turn and assigns whichever turn overlaps it most, not whichever comes first — a segment spanning a speaker change is common (Whisper and pyannote don't segment identically), and majority overlap is a better signal than segment order. Consecutive segments assigned to the same speaker are merged into one line, so one person's several short Whisper segments don't produce a wall of repeated labels. A segment with no overlapping turn at all (silence, an edge case near a boundary) is labeled "Unknown" rather than guessed.

docs.title: Summarization: map-reduce, not refine
docs.text:
A 60-minute meeting can produce a transcript well beyond what's comfortable to summarize in a single model call, and naive approaches to handling that have a specific, easy-to-miss failure mode worth documenting.

Refine-style summarization — repeatedly updating one running summary as new transcript arrives — has a well-known problem: each pass is dominated by whatever's newest, and details from early in the source material get diluted through repeated summarize-of-a-summary passes. Over many iterations, early decisions and action items can quietly disappear.

This app uses map-reduce instead:

flowchart TD
    T["Full transcript"] --> C1["Chunk 1"] & C2["Chunk 2"] & C3["Chunk N..."]
    C1 --> M1["Mini-summary 1"]
    C2 --> M2["Mini-summary 2"]
    C3 --> M3["Mini-summary N"]
    M1 & M2 & M3 --> G{"More than one\ngroup of chunks?"}
    G -- "no (short/moderate)" --> R["Final reduce:\nstructured notes"]
    G -- "yes (long meeting)" --> I["Intermediate reduce:\nconsolidate each group,\nno further compression"]
    I --> R
    R --> OUT["Key Points / Decisions / Action Items"]
  1. Map: the transcript is split into chunks (by sentence boundaries, targeting ~4000 characters each). Each chunk is summarized independently into a compact, stateless bullet-point mini-summary. A garbled or unusual chunk only pollutes its own mini-summary, not the whole document.
  2. Reduce: the mini-summaries (not the raw transcript) are combined into one final structured-notes pass.

Short transcripts that fit in a single chunk skip the map step entirely and go straight to the reduce prompt on the raw text — no unnecessary complexity for the common case.

docs.title: Why a hierarchical reduce for long meetings
docs.text:
The original assumption here was that combining mini-summaries is always cheap — a dozen chunk-summaries is a trivial amount of text against the model's context window, so a single reduce call should be able to just handle it. That assumption was directly measured and found wrong: for a genuinely long meeting (a real ~90-minute lab meeting, 89,900 characters, splitting into 23 chunks), the combined chunk-summaries totaled only ~4,950 tokens — comfortably under the model's 16,384-token context window — yet a single reduce call over all 23 still produced a summary that covered only the first ~40% of the meeting, silently dropping entire topics from the back half. This is a real behavior of long, open-ended single-pass synthesis (a known LLM tendency to underweight later items in a long unstructured list), not a token-budget problem — increasing num_ctx alone does not fix it.

The fix, validated the same way (measured on the same real transcript, not assumed): once there's more than one group of chunks (group_items(), default group size 6), each group first goes through an intermediate reduce that explicitly consolidates without compressing further — merge and de-duplicate, but don't shorten. Only the resulting (few) group-summaries go into the final structuring pass, which is also told explicitly how many parts there are and instructed to make sure every part with real content is represented, not just the earliest ones. On the same test transcript, this took the final summary from covering roughly 40% of the meeting to surfacing specific, previously entirely-missing content verbatim (down to exact figures mentioned in the meeting). Short and moderate meetings (one group) are unaffected — same single reduce call as before, just with the added numbering/coverage instruction.

Summarization calls also now pass num_ctx explicitly (main.py's SUMMARY_NUM_CTX) rather than relying on the Ollama server's Modelfile default — not the cause of the bug above, but a real gap: behavior was previously silently dependent on server-side configuration that could change.

docs.title: Wiki lookup and web search: opt-in tools, additive not exclusive
docs.text:
The Chat tab can look up pages on the lab's internal MediaWiki (wiki2.bio2.rwth-aachen.de) via an opt-in 🔎 Wiki checkbox, and separately search the public web via an opt-in 🌐 Web Search checkbox (below). Both are handled by one generalized tool-calling loop (main.answer_with_tools) that offers whichever tool schemas are currently checked — either, both, or neither — rather than two separate code paths. Wiki lookup was built first and originally had its own dedicated function; it was generalized once web search needed the exact same non-streaming, bounded, opt-in shape, rather than duplicating that machinery a second time.

Why not Ollama's own hosted web_search/web_fetch tools for the wiki. Ollama offers cloud-hosted search tools, but both route every request through ollama.com's own servers — which have no path into the lab's internal network and could never reach an on-site or VPN-only wiki. Using them would have meant an external account, an API key, and a capability that structurally cannot do the one thing actually needed. wiki.py instead talks to the wiki directly: no cloud dependency, no account, no key, nothing that isn't already true of reaching the lab's own Ollama server.

Non-streaming, and opt-in rather than always-on. Regular Chat messages stream token-by-token, as they always have. Tool-calling needs tools on the request, and agent.py's own query_ollama_chat already established (for the Agent tab) that reliably detecting tool_calls mid-stream isn't something to rely on — so a lookup-enabled turn switches to the same non-streaming request shape Agent already uses, gets its answer as one complete round trip, then reveals it all at once. Making tools a permanent part of every Chat request would have forced every message onto that non-streaming path for the sake of a capability most messages never need — so both tools are gated behind checkboxes instead, checked per-message and reset after send (like attachments, not a standing mode like Agent's Planning/Auto toggle), so only turns that actually ask for a lookup pay that cost.

The domain boundary is structural, not a permission check. The wiki tool builds its request from WIKI_BASE_URL (a fixed http://wiki2.bio2.rwth-aachen.de/index.php/ string) plus an escaped page title the model supplies — there's no way for a page title to redirect the request to a different host, the same way agent.resolve_scoped_path structurally can't be escaped by a crafted file path. http, deliberately not https: the wiki's TLS certificate is issued for a different hostname than the one it's actually reached at, so forcing HTTPS breaks the connection outright.

Extraction uses the standard library, not a new dependency. MediaWiki's HTML is well-understood and stable enough that html.parser.HTMLParser scoped to <div id="mw-content-text"> (with mw-editsection/printfooter chrome stripped, since those live inside that div rather than being excluded automatically like the surrounding navigation) does the job in about 60 lines — matching this project's pattern of only adding a dependency for something the standard library genuinely can't do.

Failure is graceful, matching diarization's precedent. A nonexistent page title (or an unreachable wiki) raises wiki.WikiError, which becomes the tool's result message rather than a crash — the model sees the failure and explains it in the reply, the same "degrade, don't fail hard" shape already used when a diarization run fails on an otherwise-successful transcription. websearch.WebSearchError follows the identical pattern for search failures.

docs.title: Web search: SearXNG on the lab network, not a cloud API
docs.text:
Unlike the wiki (internal-only, unreachable from ollama.com's cloud), general web search could have used Ollama's hosted web_search tool — reaching the public internet isn't a routing problem the way reaching an internal wiki is. It was still built the same way as the wiki tool instead: websearch.py talks directly to a SearXNG instance running on the lab network (the same server hosting Ollama), rather than through a third-party cloud API.

Why keep it in-house rather than use Ollama's hosted tool. Every other network-facing part of this app either stays fully local (speech-to-text) or reaches only the lab's own infrastructure (Ollama, the wiki) — no query text has ever left the lab network by design. Routing web search through ollama.com's cloud service would have been the first exception to that, sending chat query text to a third party for a capability the lab can self-host just as easily. websearch.py keeps that property intact: SearXNG is a metasearch engine the lab runs itself, so the app's own network boundary stays exactly where it's always been.

This means SearXNG has to be reachable from wherever BrainLabLLM runs, not just from the server hosting it. SEARXNG_URL in websearch.py points at the lab server's address, not localhost — SearXNG's own bind address has to be configured to accept connections from other lab machines (matching how the Ollama server itself is already reachable network-wide, not just locally), which is a deliberate infrastructure decision made once, not something websearch.py can work around on its own.

docs.title: Concurrency model
docs.text:
The UI runs on Tkinter's single main thread, as it must. Every potentially slow operation — model loading, transcription, network requests to the AI server — runs on a background threading.Thread, with results marshaled back to the main thread via root.after(0, ...), which is the only thread-safe way to touch Tkinter widgets from outside the main thread.

A recurring pattern throughout the codebase is a generation token: an integer that's incremented every time a new operation starts (a new chat message sent, a new recording started, a new summarization triggered). Callbacks from a background thread check their captured token against the current one before touching the UI — if they don't match, a newer operation has superseded this one, and the stale callback is silently discarded. This is what makes "click Stop then immediately click Record again" or "start a new chat while a reply is still streaming" safe, without needing to actually cancel in-flight network requests or threads.

docs.title: Agent: approval-gated tool calling
docs.text:
The Agent tab is built on Ollama's OpenAI-style tool calling: AgentSession sends the running conversation plus a list of tool schemas to /api/chat, the model responds with either plain text (done) or a tool_calls list naming a function and its arguments, agent.py executes the requested tool and feeds the result back as a role: "tool" message, and the cycle repeats until the model stops asking for tools or a hard iteration cap (MAX_ITERATIONS = 20) is hit. Planning and Auto mode share this one loop — they only differ in what happens when the model asks to change something.

Every mutating action is approval-gated, with no "fully autonomous" option, for two reasons specific to this app's context: it's meant to be usable by people with no coding background who can't be expected to review code well enough to trust a model's judgment about when something is safe, and this project's own earlier attempt at unattended LLM-driven coding (aider, documented in Development) hallucinated non-existent APIs when left to work without tight, continuous supervision — a smaller local model making autonomous multi-step decisions on someone's actual files is exactly the failure mode to design against, not just a hypothetical risk.

  • Planning mode lets the model use read-only tools freely, but a proposed write_file/edit_file call is only ever turned into a diff for display — the file is never touched. This is implemented as a genuine interception, not a UI-layer suggestion: the write path is never called.
  • Auto mode runs the same loop, but a mutating tool call blocks the background thread on a threading.Event and shows the user the exact diff or shell command before it can proceed — reusing the same root.after(0, ...) + token-check pattern described above, so the Tk main loop is never touched while waiting. A rejection is fed back to the model as a tool result explaining the change was declined, so it adapts instead of silently retrying the same thing.

The project-folder boundary is enforced structurally, not just suggested to the model. Every file tool routes through resolve_scoped_path, which rejects absolute paths outright and resolves symlinks before checking containment (os.path.realpath + os.path.commonpath, not a startswith check, which has a well-known prefix bug). This means a malicious or simply mistaken tool call — asking to read ../../something — is blocked before it reaches the filesystem, regardless of what mode the session is in or whether the user would have approved it. run_shell_command is the one exception this boundary can't fully cover: a shell command can cd or use absolute paths internally no matter what cwd it's given, which is exactly why that tool is Auto-mode-only and its safety comes entirely from mandatory human approval of the literal command string, not from path scoping.

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: See Building from Source and Packaging & Distribution for how the app is turned into a distributable installer, including why the speech model is bundled offline and how GPU/CPU fallback is made robust across unknown lab hardware.

docs.title: v1.0.0 — 2026-07-28
docs.text:
Initial release.

Chat

  • Streaming chat against a local Ollama server, with conversation history and a sidebar for switching between past conversations
  • Markdown-lite rendering (bold, inline code, fenced code blocks)
  • Regenerate and copy-last-reply actions
  • File attachments — attach text-based files (code, logs, notes) for the model to read as part of your message

Meetings

  • Microphone selection with a persisted preference and a one-click Test Microphone check
  • Record-then-transcribe pipeline using a locally-bundled faster-whisper model — fully offline, with automatic GPU acceleration and CPU fallback
  • Map-reduce summarization into structured notes (Key Points / Decisions / Action Items), scaling to arbitrarily long meetings
  • Export to .txt and save-to-chat-history

Distribution

  • Self-contained installer requiring no Python, conda, or command-line use
  • Speech-to-text model bundled for fully offline transcription out of the box
  • Configuration via a plain-text config.json for lab administrators, and an in-app Settings dialog for day-to-day server address changes

Design

  • A custom visual theme (dark sidebar, color-coded action states, message bubbles) rather than default Tk styling

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Most settings can be changed from File → Settings in the app (see Settings). This page documents the underlying config.json file, for lab administrators setting up a new machine or troubleshooting.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
config.json sits in the same folder as BrainLabLLM.exe (wherever the app was installed — by default %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\BrainLabLLM\). It's created automatically with default values the first time the app runs, if it doesn't already exist.

It's a plain text file — open it with Notepad, edit, save, and restart the app.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
config.json
{
  "ollama_api_url": "http://10.3.2.112:11434/api/chat",
  "ollama_model": "qwen3.6:35b-coder",
  "whisper_model_size": "medium",
  "whisper_device": "auto"
}
Field Default Description ollama_api_url (lab-specific) Full URL to your Ollama server's /api/chat endpoint. Same as the Server Address field in Settings. ollama_model (lab-specific) Model name to request from that server. Same as the Model Name field in Settings. whisper_model_size medium Which faster-whisper model size to use for transcription. The installed app bundles the medium model's weights for fully offline use — changing this to a size that isn't bundled will make the app try to download it from Hugging Face Hub on first use, which requires internet access. whisper_device auto Controls GPU/CPU selection for transcription. auto tries the GPU first and falls back to CPU automatically if unavailable (recommended for shared lab machines with unknown hardware). cuda forces GPU use and fails loudly if none is available, rather than silently using CPU — useful for confirming GPU setup during installation. cpu forces CPU-only, useful for machines you know don't have a usable GPU, since it skips a few seconds of GPU-detection overhead on every recording.

docs.title: Per-user data
docs.text: Chat history and your last-selected microphone are stored separately from config.json, in %APPDATA%\BrainLabLLM\ (chats.json and settings.json). This is deliberate: the app's install folder may not be writable by every user (especially if installed to a shared or admin-managed location), while %APPDATA% is always writable by the current user and keeps each person's history private on a shared machine.

docs.title: Resetting to defaults
docs.text: Delete config.json and restart the app — a fresh one with default values will be created automatically.

docs.title: "Windows protected your PC"
docs.text: This is expected for any brand-new, unsigned program — it's a reputation check (SmartScreen), not a malware detection. Click More info, then Run anyway. It only appears once.

docs.title: Antivirus flags or quarantines the installer
docs.text: Also common for new, unsigned software. If your antivirus quarantines it, restore it from quarantine, or ask IT to allowlist it. If you'd like independent confirmation it's clean, you can scan it yourself with Windows Defender or upload the file to a service like VirusTotal.

docs.title: "Setup files missing" when running the installer
docs.text: The installer (BrainLabLLMSetup.exe) needs the BrainLabLLM folder sitting in the same directory as itself. If you moved or renamed just the .exe, re-extract the original .zip and run it from there without moving anything first.

docs.title: The transcript comes back empty every time
docs.text:
This is almost always a muted or wrong microphone — recording silently "succeeds" even with no audio, so there's no error to see. Go to the Meeting tab and click Test Microphone:

  • If it reports no sound detected, check:
    1. The correct device is selected in the dropdown (a webcam mic and a headset mic can both show up — make sure you picked the one that's actually connected/in use)
    2. Windows Sound settings → Recording tab → confirm the device isn't muted and its level isn't at 0
    3. You were actually speaking during the 2.5-second test

docs.title: My microphone doesn't appear in the dropdown
docs.text: Click into the Meeting tab again to refresh the device list (it's read fresh from Windows each time the app builds that screen). If it's a USB device, try unplugging and replugging it, and confirm Windows itself sees it (Settings → System → Sound).

docs.title: Fast or continuous speech produces garbled or fragmented text
docs.text: This should no longer happen — an earlier design that transcribed live while recording had exactly this problem, which is why the app now transcribes the whole recording in one pass after you stop. See Architecture for why. If you're still seeing fragmented results, please report it — this would be a regression.

docs.title: Transcription always uses CPU, never GPU, even though this machine has a graphics card
docs.text: The app tries the GPU automatically and falls back to CPU if it can't be used (outdated driver, unsupported card, or a hung/broken CUDA setup). This is intentional — CPU is slower but always works, so the app prefers "slow but working" over "fast but crashes." If you want to confirm what's going wrong, an administrator can set "whisper_device": "cuda" in config.json (see Configuration) to force GPU use and see the actual error instead of silently falling back.

docs.title: "Can't reach the AI server"
docs.text: You're most likely not connected to the lab network. Connect via VPN or on-site, then try again. Use File → Settings → Test Connection to confirm.

docs.title: The AI server address changed and now nothing works
docs.text: Open File → Settings, update the Server address, click Test Connection to confirm it works, then Save and restart the app. See Settings.

docs.title: Web Search says it can't reach the search service
docs.text: Web search runs through a separate service on the lab network, independent of the AI server itself — being connected to the lab network for normal chat doesn't guarantee this service is also reachable. If regular chat and wiki lookup work fine but web search specifically doesn't, this is most likely that service being down or not reachable from your machine; report it to whoever manages this tool for your lab rather than assuming it's something you can fix from Settings.

docs.title: A file I tried to attach was rejected
docs.text: Only text-based files are supported (source code, .txt, .md, config files, logs, etc.) — the AI model reads text, not images or binary formats like .pdf or .docx. Very large files (over roughly 200 KB) are truncated rather than rejected outright; a truncated attachment is marked as such.

docs.title: The app won't start at all
docs.text: Check Task Manager for a lingering BrainLabLLM.exe process from a previous crash and end it, then try launching again. If that doesn't help, try reinstalling — running the setup installer again is safe and will overwrite the existing install.

docs.title: I want to see my old chat history but reinstalled the app
docs.text: Chat history lives in %APPDATA%\BrainLabLLM\chats.json, separate from the app's install folder, so a normal reinstall (installing over the same location) doesn't touch it. If you're moving to a new machine, copy that file across manually.

docs.title: Still stuck?
docs.text: Check the Configuration reference in case a setting is misconfigured, or reach out to whoever manages this tool for your lab.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Windows 10/11
  • Miniconda or Anaconda
  • A local Ollama server reachable on your network, running a chat-capable model

docs.title: Set up the environment
docs.text:
conda create -n aider_env python=3.11 -y
conda activate aider_env
pip install requests sounddevice soundfile scipy numpy faster-whisper truststore pytest
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
pip install pyannote.audio

Windows SSL certificate bug

If pip install intermittently fails with ASN1: NOT_ENOUGH_DATA or similar SSL errors, this is a known CPython-on-Windows bug where a single malformed certificate in the Windows certificate store crashes Python's default SSL context. Installing truststore and adding a sitecustomize.py alongside your environment's site-packages containing:

import truststore
truststore.inject_into_ssl()

routes around it. One caveat: this can conflict with pip's own vendored copy of truststore during large dependency resolutions (a RecursionError deep in SSL handling) — if that happens, temporarily rename sitecustomize.py for the duration of the pip install, then restore it.

torch must be the CUDA build, not CPU-only

Plain pip install torch grabs a CPU-only wheel, which makes torch.cuda.is_available() return False even with a working GPU — this silently breaks speaker identification (see Architecture), since it's gated on that check. Always install torch from the cu1xx index matching your driver, as shown above (check with nvidia-smi; the index only needs to be at or below what your driver supports, not an exact match).

Speaker identification needs a Hugging Face token in dev mode

pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1 is a gated model — accept its terms at huggingface.co and generate a token at hf.co/settings/tokens, then set HUGGINGFACE_TOKEN in your environment before running from source. This is a one-time step for whoever builds the packaged app: the model gets bundled into the exe the same way the Whisper model is, so end users never need a token or an account.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
python main.py

config.json and chats.json will be created automatically on first run (see Configuration).

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
BrainLabLLM/
├── main.py           # Tkinter UI, chat networking, summarization
├── meeting.py         # Audio recording + transcription (no UI dependency)
├── diarization.py      # Speaker identification (no UI dependency)
├── agent.py             # Coding-agent tool-calling loop (no UI dependency)
├── wiki.py               # Lab wiki lookup tool (no UI dependency)
├── websearch.py            # Public web search tool via local SearXNG (no UI dependency)
├── theme.py                  # Color palette + ttk.Style setup
├── installer.py                # Standalone installer GUI (built separately)
├── app_icon.ico                  # App icon, used for both the exe and window icon
├── tests/                          # Automated pytest suite
├── packaging/                     # Tracked sources for files assembled into dist/ at build time
├── mkdocs.yml                       # This documentation site's configuration
└── docs/                              # This documentation site's content

docs.title: Running the standalone test scripts
docs.text:
meeting.py includes a _console_test() function for validating the audio → transcription pipeline without the GUI:

python meeting.py

This records from your default microphone for 30 seconds and prints the transcript — useful for isolating microphone or GPU issues from UI issues.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Packaging & Distribution — turning this into the installer end users get
  • Contributing — code conventions and how to propose changes

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This is an internal lab tool, but it's built to be easy to extend. A few notes for anyone picking it up.

docs.title: Code conventions
docs.text:
• No comments explaining what code does — names should make that obvious. Comments are reserved for why, when it isn't otherwise obvious (a workaround for a specific bug, a non-obvious constraint, a design trade-off).
  • Threading pattern: any operation that could block (network calls, model loading, transcription) runs on a threading.Thread, with results delivered back to the UI via root.after(0, callback, ...). Never touch a Tkinter widget from a background thread directly.
  • Generation tokens: when adding a new cancellable/restartable operation, follow the existing pattern (generation_token in ChatApp, recording_token / meeting_summary_token) — increment an integer when a new operation starts, capture it in the background thread, and check it still matches before applying results to the UI. See Architecture.
  • Friendly errors: user-facing error messages should go through friendly_error_message() in main.py rather than showing raw exception text, for anything that could plausibly happen to a non-technical user (network errors especially).

docs.title: Testing changes
docs.text:
agent.py has a real automated test suite under tests/ (pytest) — path scoping, the read/write/edit/search/shell tools, diff computation, and AgentSession's control flow (Planning vs. Auto mode, approve/reject, cancellation, the iteration cap, path-escape attempts). Run it with:

pip install pytest
pytest tests/

Most tests are fast and don't touch the network. A handful (tests/test_agent_live.py, the classes marked @requires_lab_server) exercise the real tool-calling loop against the lab Ollama server and are skipped automatically with a clear reason if that server isn't reachable — this is deliberate: agent.py is tkinter-free by design (see Architecture), which is exactly what makes it practical to test this way, unlike the Tkinter UI layer below.

main.py, meeting.py, and the UI layer in general don't have an automated suite — the practical approach used throughout development instead:

  • meeting.py changes: test with python meeting.py (the built-in console test) before touching the UI, to isolate audio/transcription bugs from UI bugs.
  • UI changes: drive ChatApp methods directly from a throwaway script rather than clicking through manually — for example:
import tkinter as tk
import main

root = tk.Tk()
app = main.ChatApp(root)
app._add_user_message("test")
app._render_history()
# ...assert on app.history.get("1.0", tk.END), widget states, etc.
root.destroy()

This is dramatically faster to iterate on than manual clicking, and is how the layout/styling/threading bugs documented in Architecture were actually found and fixed.

  • After any change touching meeting.py or the recording flow: test with a real microphone and real speech before considering it done — silent failures (like the muted-mic issue documented in Troubleshooting) don't show up in code review or unit-style tests.
  • Before a release: rebuild the full installer (see Packaging) and test the actual installed .exe, not just python main.py — packaging-specific bugs (missing DLLs, bundled model path resolution) only show up in the built artifact.

docs.title: Making changes to the documentation site
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme. To preview changes locally:

pip install mkdocs-material mkdocs-mermaid2-plugin
mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Pushing to the repository's default branch deploys automatically via the GitHub Actions workflow in .github/workflows/docs.yml.

docs.title: Proposing changes
docs.text: Open a pull request. For anything touching the recording/transcription pipeline or the packaging process, please describe what you tested it with (real mic + real speech, or the specific machine/GPU configuration) in the PR description — those are exactly the areas where changes that look correct in code review have historically failed in practice.

docs.title: Packaging & Distribution
docs.text: How the app becomes the .zip package end users download — including several non-obvious gotchas that cost real debugging time, documented here so they don't have to be rediscovered.

docs.title: Design goals
docs.text:
1. Zero coding experience required to install or run it.
  2. Fully offline speech-to-text — no lab machine should need internet access just to transcribe a meeting.
  3. No new software required on the build machine beyond what's already needed to develop the app — deliberately avoided pulling in a separate installer-building tool (see why).

docs.title: Building the app bundle
docs.text:
The app is packaged with PyInstaller in --onedir mode (not --onefile) — with ~6 GB of bundled model weights and DLLs (most of it PyTorch's CUDA runtime, needed for speaker identification), --onefile's startup-time self-extraction to a temp directory would add meaningful launch latency on every run; --onedir pays that cost once, at install time, instead.

Build command (run from the project root)
pyinstaller --name BrainLabLLM --onedir --windowed --noconfirm --noupx \
  --icon app_icon.ico \
  --add-data "<path-to-cached-whisper-medium-model>;whisper_model" \
  --add-data "<path-to-cached-pyannote-diarization-model>;diarization_model" \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\tcl86t.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\tk86t.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\liblzma.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\libbz2.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi-7.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi-8.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\libexpat.dll;." \
  --collect-all ctranslate2 \
  --collect-all faster_whisper \
  --collect-all onnxruntime \
  --collect-all tokenizers \
  --collect-all huggingface_hub \
  --collect-all torch \
  --collect-all torchaudio \
  --collect-all torchcodec \
  --collect-all pyannote.audio \
  --collect-all pyannote.core \
  --collect-all pyannote.database \
  --collect-all pyannote.pipeline \
  --collect-all pyannote.metrics \
  --collect-all pyannoteai_sdk \
  --collect-all asteroid_filterbanks \
  main.py

--noupx: don't compress the CUDA DLLs

UPX compression is skipped for this build. torch's bundled CUDA runtime (cublas, cudnn, cusparse, cufft, cusolver) is already ~4 GB of dense binary — compressing it buys little, adds real time to every build, and UPX has a history of flaky interaction with large, complex DLLs. Simpler to just not risk it for marginal savings.

docs.title: Why the explicit --add-binary DLLs
docs.text:
PyInstaller's automatic dependency scanner, when run from a conda environment on Windows, does not reliably find tcl86t.dll / tk86t.dll (needed for Tkinter itself) or a handful of other C-extension dependencies (liblzma, libbz2, ffi, libexpat) — they live in <conda-env>\Library\bin\, a location PyInstaller's scanner doesn't check by default when building from a conda Python, as opposed to a "vanilla" python.org install where these ship alongside the interpreter itself.

Symptom if you skip this: the built .exe fails immediately with ImportError: DLL load failed while importing _tkinter (or _ctypes, depending on which DLL is missing), even though the exact same code runs fine with python main.py in the dev environment. The build log itself gives a hint — look for WARNING: Library not found: could not resolve '...' lines.

docs.title: Bundling the speech model for offline use
docs.text:
faster-whisper normally downloads model weights from Hugging Face Hub on first use and caches them locally. To avoid every lab machine needing internet access (and to avoid a slow first-run download on a shared/proxied network), the model's cache directory is bundled directly into the app via --add-data, and meeting.py's resolve_model_path() checks sys.frozen to decide whether to load from the bundled local path or fall back to the Hugging Face model name (dev mode only):

def resolve_model_path(model_size):
    if getattr(sys, "frozen", False):
        bundled = os.path.join(sys._MEIPASS, "whisper_model")
        if os.path.isdir(bundled):
            return bundled
    return model_size

faster-whisper's WhisperModel(...) constructor accepts either a Hugging Face model name or a local directory path containing the converted model files (model.bin, config.json, tokenizer.json, vocabulary.txt) — this is what makes the swap possible without touching the loading code itself.

docs.title: Bundling the speaker-identification model
docs.text:
The same pattern is reused for pyannote/speaker-diarization-community-1 (see Architecture for why this model specifically): its cache directory is bundled via --add-data ...;diarization_model, and diarization.py's resolve_diarization_model_path() checks sys.frozen the same way resolve_model_path() does, falling back to the Hugging Face repo id plus a dev-only HUGGINGFACE_TOKEN (see Building from Source) when running unfrozen. pyannote.audio's Pipeline.from_pretrained(...) accepts a bare local directory path with no token needed, exactly like WhisperModel does — confirmed directly, since this is the one part of the frozen build that's easy to get subtly wrong without testing it.

This is a much heavier addition than the speech model: torch's CUDA runtime alone is roughly 4 GB (cublas, cudnn, cusparse, cufft, cusolver — the actual math libraries GPU tensor ops need, not something safely prunable). That's a deliberate, discussed trade-off, not an oversight — see Installation for the resulting download size end users see. The alternative (a separate, optional "with Speaker ID" build) was considered and rejected in favor of keeping a single installer simple to build, test, and hand out, at the cost of every install carrying weight that machines without a GPU can never use.

docs.title: GPU/CPU robustness across unknown hardware
docs.text:
Lab machines vary — some have a capable GPU, some don't, some have one with an outdated driver. MeetingSession._ensure_model_loaded() handles this in two layers:

  1. A try/except around GPU model construction and a warmup transcription call, falling back to CPU on any exception.
  2. A timeout, not just an exception handler: GPU initialization runs on its own thread and is joined with a timeout. A plain try/except can't catch a hang — and a genuinely broken driver/CUDA combination can hang rather than raise a clean error. If GPU init doesn't complete within 30 seconds, the app proceeds on CPU regardless, leaving the stuck thread to die on its own in the background (it's a daemon thread).

config.json's whisper_device setting (auto / cuda / cpu) lets an administrator override this behavior per-machine if needed — see Configuration.

docs.title: The installer
docs.text:
Rather than a separate installer-building tool, installer.py is a small, dependency-free Tkinter GUI, built with PyInstaller the same way as the main app (--onefile, since it has no heavy dependencies of its own). It still uses Tkinter, so it needs the same conda-env DLL fix as the main app — skipping it produces an installer that crashes immediately with DLL load failed while importing _tkinter:

pyinstaller --name BrainLabLLMSetup --onefile --windowed --noconfirm \
  --icon app_icon.ico \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\tcl86t.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\tk86t.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\liblzma.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\libbz2.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi-7.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\ffi-8.dll;." \
  --add-binary "<conda-env>\Library\bin\libexpat.dll;." \
  installer.py

It expects the built BrainLabLLM folder to sit next to it, copies it to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\BrainLabLLM\ (a per-user location — no administrator rights needed), and creates Desktop and Start Menu shortcuts via a small PowerShell WScript.Shell COM call (no extra Python packages required for that either).

docs.title: Why not Inno Setup or a similar tool
docs.text: A more conventional approach would use a dedicated installer-authoring tool. That was deliberately avoided here: it would require downloading and installing new third-party software onto the build machine, which is a meaningfully different kind of action than installing a Python package via pip for development purposes, and isn't something to do without an explicit go-ahead. A minimal hand-rolled installer using only what's already needed to build the app (PyInstaller, Tkinter) sidesteps that entirely while still producing a normal-feeling double-click installer experience.

docs.title: Assembling the distributable
docs.text:
The plain-language end-user README.txt is tracked in source at packaging/README.txt (the dist/ folder itself is gitignored, so anything only living there is lost on a clean rebuild) — copy it in before zipping:

Copy-Item 'packaging\README.txt' 'dist\README.txt' -Force
Compress-Archive -Path 'dist\BrainLabLLM', 'dist\BrainLabLLMSetup.exe', 'dist\README.txt' `
  -DestinationPath 'dist\BrainLabLLM_Setup_Package.zip' -Force

The result — BrainLabLLMSetup.exe sitting next to the BrainLabLLM folder, plus the plain-language README.txt — is what gets shared with lab members. See Installation for the end-user side of this.

docs.title: Expect Windows SmartScreen and antivirus warnings
docs.text: Because the resulting .exe files aren't code-signed, Windows SmartScreen will show a "protected your PC" warning on first run on any machine — this is a reputation check based on how many times a given file hash has been seen, not a malware verdict, and is unavoidable without a paid code-signing certificate. Similarly, some antivirus products flag new, unsigned, PyInstaller-built executables heuristically. Neither indicates an actual problem; both are documented for end users in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: First-Time Setup
docs.text: Most users don't need to change anything — the app ships pre-configured to talk to your lab's AI server. This page covers what actually happens behind the scenes on first launch, and the handful of things worth checking.

docs.title: What happens on first launch
docs.text:
1. A config.json file is created next to the installed app (if one doesn't already exist), containing the default server address, model name, and speech settings. See Configuration for the full reference.
  2. A per-user data folder is created at %APPDATA%\BrainLabLLM\ for your chat history and preferences — kept separate from the install location so it survives reinstalls and works even though the app itself is installed somewhere you might not have write access to.
  3. On the Meeting tab, the app picks a default microphone automatically. Your device names are populated live from Windows — nothing needs to be pre-configured.

docs.title: Check your microphone once
docs.text: Before your first real meeting, switch to the Meeting tab and click Test Microphone. This catches the single most common first-run problem: a muted or wrong microphone, which otherwise fails silently (recording "succeeds" but the transcript comes back empty, with no error).

docs.title: Confirm you can reach the AI server
docs.text: Open File → Settings and click Test Connection. If it fails, you're most likely not on the lab network — connect via VPN or on-site and try again. This doesn't affect the Meeting tab's transcription, which works fully offline.

docs.title: GPU or CPU?
docs.text:
If your machine has a supported NVIDIA GPU, the app uses it automatically for much faster transcription (a few seconds instead of tens of seconds for a short recording). This is fully automatic — after your first recording completes, look for the Whisper: GPU or Whisper: CPU label next to the Record button to see which one was used. There's nothing to configure unless you want to force one or the other; see Configuration.

Transcription itself works fine on CPU. Identifying speakers is different: it requires a GPU, with no CPU fallback. The 🗣 Identify speakers checkbox on the Meeting tab is disabled automatically on machines without one — see Identifying speakers.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: No coding experience, Python, or command-line use is required. This takes about a minute.

docs.title: 1. Get the installer package
docs.text: Ask whoever manages the tool for your lab for BrainLabLLM_Setup_Package.zip (it's typically shared over the lab network or a shared drive — it's roughly 4.5 GB, since it includes the speech-to-text model and the (optional, GPU-only) speaker-identification model so you don't need internet access later).

docs.title: 2. Unzip it
docs.text:
Right-click the .zip file and choose Extract All. You'll get a folder containing:

BrainLabLLM_Setup_Package/
├── BrainLabLLMSetup.exe   ← run this
├── BrainLabLLM/           ← the app itself (don't move or rename)
└── README.txt

Keep the setup file and the app folder together

BrainLabLLMSetup.exe looks for the BrainLabLLM folder sitting right next to it. If you move the .exe on its own, installation will fail with a "setup files missing" message.

docs.title: 3. Run the installer
docs.text:
Double-click BrainLabLLMSetup.exe.

About the Windows warning screen

The first time you run it, Windows will very likely show a blue "Windows protected your PC" screen. This happens for any brand-new program that isn't yet widely downloaded — it's a reputation check, not a malware detection. Click More info, then Run anyway. You'll only see this once.

You'll see a small setup window:

  • Install location is shown (no need to change it — it installs to your own user profile, so no administrator rights are needed)
  • Leave Create a Desktop shortcut and Launch after installing checked (recommended)
  • Click Install

A progress bar copies the app (this takes a few minutes, mostly depending on your disk — the speaker-identification model alone is a few gigabytes), then shortcuts appear on your Desktop and in the Start Menu.

docs.title: 4. That's it
docs.text:
No restart, no additional downloads, no accounts. Speech recognition works completely offline; you'll only need the lab network once you start chatting or generating summaries.

Continue to the Quick Start to try it out.

docs.title: For developers: building from source
docs.text: If you're setting this up on a new lab machine and need to build the installer yourself (rather than reusing an existing package), see Building from Source.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Two things to try first: a chat message, and a recorded meeting.

docs.title: Your first chat message
docs.text:
1. Open BrainLabLLM from your Desktop or Start Menu.
  2. You'll land on the Chat tab.
  3. Type a message in the box at the bottom and press Enter (use Shift+Enter for a new line without sending).
  4. The reply streams in as it's generated.

That's the whole workflow. A few things worth knowing:

  • New chat (top of the sidebar) starts a fresh conversation. Old conversations stay in the sidebar — click any of them to go back.
  • The 📎 button next to the input box lets you attach a file (code, logs, notes) so the model can see its contents.
  • If a reply is taking a while, the Send button becomes Stop — click it to cancel.

docs.title: Your first recorded meeting
docs.text:
1. Switch to the Meeting tab.
  2. Check the Microphone dropdown is set to the right device. If you're not sure, click Test Microphone and say something — it'll tell you plainly whether it picked up sound.
  3. Click ● Record, then talk normally. There's no live transcript while recording — that's intentional (see why).
  4. Click ⏹ Stop when you're done. The whole recording gets transcribed in one pass, which takes a few seconds for a short meeting.
  5. Once the transcript appears, click ✨ Summarize for structured notes (Key Points / Decisions / Action Items).
  6. Use 💾 Save to chat history to keep it in the sidebar, or 📤 Export .txt to save it as a plain text file you can share.

First recording is a little slower

The speech-to-text model loads into memory the first time you record after opening the app — you'll see "Loading model..." for a few seconds. Every recording after that is faster.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Chat features in depth
  • Meeting features in depth
  • Change the AI server address

docs.title: Agent
docs.text: The Agent tab lets the same local model act as a coding assistant against a project folder on your machine — reading files, proposing edits, and (if you let it) running commands. Nothing it does is invisible: every change it wants to make is shown to you before it happens.

docs.title: Choosing a project folder
docs.text: Click Browse... and pick the folder you want the agent to work in. It can only see and touch files inside that folder — anything outside it (including going "up" with .. or giving an absolute path elsewhere on your machine) is refused automatically, even if the agent tries. Your last-used folder is remembered between sessions.

docs.title: Planning vs. Auto
docs.text:
Two modes, chosen with the radio buttons above the transcript:

  • Planning — the agent can freely read files and search the project to understand it, but any change it wants to make is only ever shown to you as a proposed diff. Nothing is written to disk in this mode. Use this to see what the agent would do before committing to anything.
  • Auto — the agent can actually make changes and run commands, but it stops and asks before every single one. You'll see the exact diff (for a file edit) or the exact command (for a shell command) and have to click Approve or Reject before it proceeds. There's no "run everything unattended" option — this is deliberate.

If you reject a proposed change, the agent is told you declined it and adapts — it won't just try the identical change again.

docs.title: Working with it
docs.text:
Describe what you want in the input box and press Enter (or Send). The transcript shows the agent's reasoning as it happens:

  • 📄 / 📁 / 🔍 icons mark it reading a file, listing a folder, or searching code — these never need approval, since they can't change anything.
  • ✏️ marks a proposed file edit — shown as a diff, colored like a standard patch (green additions, red removals).
  • 💻 marks a shell command — shown as the literal command that would run.

Click ⏹ Stop at any time to cancel a run in progress. If it was mid-way through waiting for your approval on something, stopping cancels that too — nothing gets applied.

docs.title: What it can and can't do
docs.text:
• It can read and search any file in the project folder, and propose creating, overwriting, or making a targeted edit to a file.
  • In Auto mode, it can also run shell commands (like pip install or pytest) inside the project folder — always shown to you first, always requiring approval.
  • It cannot see or touch anything outside the project folder you picked, no matter what it's asked to do.
  • Agent conversations aren't saved to your chat history the way regular chats are — they're scoped to the current session. Start a new conversation with the agent by picking a folder and sending a new instruction.

docs.title: Why it's built this way
docs.text: See Architecture for the reasoning behind approval-gating every change rather than letting the agent run fully unattended.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text: The Chat tab is a straightforward conversation interface with a few features aimed at coding and technical work.

docs.title: Sending messages
docs.text:
Type in the input box and press Enter to send. Shift+Enter inserts a line break instead of sending, for multi-line messages.

While the model is replying, the send button becomes a Stop button — click it to cancel generation early. Whatever was generated so far is kept in the conversation, marked [stopped].

docs.title: Managing conversations
docs.text:
The sidebar lists every conversation you've had, most recent first.

  • + New chat starts a fresh conversation. A conversation's title is set automatically from your first message (or the first attached file's name, if you send an attachment with no text).
  • Click any item in the sidebar to switch to it.
  • 🗑 Delete chat removes the current conversation after a confirmation prompt.

Conversations are saved automatically after every message — there's no explicit save action, and nothing is lost if the app closes unexpectedly.

docs.title: Markdown and code formatting
docs.text:
Replies are rendered with lightweight markdown support:

  • **bold** renders as bold
  • `inline code` renders in a monospace font
  • Triple-backtick fenced code blocks render as a distinct, syntax-highlight-style dark block

This means code the model writes is easy to read and copy directly from the chat.

docs.title: Regenerate and copy
docs.text:
• ↻ Regenerate discards the last reply and asks the model to try again — useful if a response wasn't quite right. Only available when the last message is from the assistant.
  • 📋 Copy last reply copies the most recent assistant response to your clipboard.

docs.title: Attaching files
docs.text:
Click the 📎 button next to the input box to attach one or more files to your next message. This lets you ask questions about a specific piece of code, a log file, or notes without pasting them in by hand.

What you can attach: any text-based file — source code, .txt, .md, .json, .csv, log files, configuration files, and similar. The content is read as plain text and included directly in your message, wrapped in a code block so it's clearly separated from your own text.

What you can't attach: binary files (images, PDFs, Word documents, executables, etc.) — the model this app talks to reads text only, so these are rejected with a message explaining why.

Size limit: each file is capped at roughly 200 KB. Larger files are truncated (and marked "truncated" on the attachment chip) so a single huge file can't push the whole conversation past the model's context window.

Once you attach a file, it appears as a small chip above the input box showing its name — click the ✕ on a chip to remove it before sending. Attachments are cleared automatically after you send.

Multiple files at once

The file picker supports selecting multiple files in one go — hold Ctrl (or Shift for a range) while selecting in the dialog.

docs.title: Looking things up on the lab wiki
docs.text:
Check 🔎 Wiki next to the input box before sending a message to let the assistant fetch a page from the lab's internal wiki (wiki2.bio2.rwth-aachen.de) if it thinks the answer is there — lab rules, procedures, equipment, protocols, and similar lab-specific topics, rather than general knowledge. Ask something like "what does the wiki say about systems neurophysiology?" and it'll look up the relevant page itself.

This only reaches that one internal wiki, nothing else on the internet — no accounts, no API keys, and nothing ever leaves the lab network. See Architecture for why this was originally built as a purpose-built tool rather than reusing general web search (below).

A couple of things worth knowing:

  • The reply arrives all at once instead of streaming, unlike a normal message. This is the trade-off for the assistant being able to decide, read a page, and then answer — reliably detecting that mid-stream isn't something this app relies on, so a lookup-enabled turn waits and reveals the complete answer instead.
  • The checkbox turns itself off after every send (like attachments) rather than staying on — so it only affects the one message you checked it for, not every message afterward.
  • If the reply used the wiki, it starts with a small 🔎 Looked up wiki page: ... note naming the page, so you can tell it wasn't just answering from general knowledge.
  • If the page doesn't exist (wrong title, typo), the assistant says so in its reply rather than showing an error — it's told about the failure and can react to it, the same way a person would if a link 404'd.

docs.title: Searching the web
docs.text:
Check 🌐 Web Search next to the input box to let the assistant search the public web to answer this message — for current information or general questions the wiki wouldn't have. It can be checked together with 🔎 Wiki on the same message if you want both consulted.

This goes through a search instance hosted on the lab network, not a third-party cloud search API — same non-streaming trade-off and same "turns itself off after sending" behavior as the wiki checkbox. If the reply used it, it starts with a 🌐 Searched the web: ... note naming the search terms used.

docs.title: Meetings
docs.text: The Meeting tab records audio, transcribes it, and can turn the transcript into structured notes — all without needing to remember to take notes yourself.

docs.title: Choosing a microphone
docs.text:
The Microphone dropdown lists every input device Windows can see. Your last choice is remembered between sessions.

Click Test Microphone any time to record 2.5 seconds and get a plain-language result: either confirmation that sound was detected (with an approximate signal level), or a warning if nothing came through — with the most likely causes listed (wrong device selected, muted, or you didn't speak during the test). This exists because a muted microphone otherwise fails silently: recording appears to work, but the transcript comes back empty with no error message.

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
Click ● Record. The button turns red and becomes ⏹ Stop, and a timer starts counting. Talk normally — there's no need to pause between sentences or speak unnaturally slowly.

Click ⏹ Stop when you're done. The status area shows progress: Stopping... → Transcribing... → Done, and the full transcript appears in the Transcript panel once processing finishes.

docs.title: Transcribing an existing recording
docs.text:
Already have an audio or video file — a recording from a phone, a webinar download, a call recorded elsewhere? Click 📁 Transcribe File... instead of Record, and pick the file. It runs through the exact same transcription (and afterward, summarization) pipeline as a live recording; the only difference is the audio comes from a file instead of a microphone. Most common formats work (wav, mp3, m4a, flac, ogg, and others) — anything the file dialog doesn't recognize can still be selected via "All files".

Recording and file transcription can't run at the same time — both buttons disable while either one is working, so there's no risk of them fighting over the same transcript.

docs.title: Why no live transcript?
docs.text:
An earlier version of this app showed the transcript incrementally while recording, using a voice-activity detector to chop speech into utterances as you talked. In testing, this broke down noticeably for fast or continuous speech: natural micro-pauses (a breath, a brief hesitation) were often mistaken for sentence breaks, fragmenting continuous thoughts mid-sentence and occasionally producing short, out-of-context clips that the speech model would fill in with plausible-sounding but wrong text.

Recording the whole thing and transcribing it in one pass — using the speech model's own, more sophisticated internal segmentation — turned out to be dramatically more reliable, at the cost of not seeing text appear while you talk. For meeting notes, accuracy matters more than a live readout, so that's the trade-off this app makes. See Architecture for the full story.

docs.title: Identifying speakers
docs.text:
Check 🗣 Identify speakers before you record or transcribe a file to label who's talking in the transcript ("Speaker 1: ...", "Speaker 2: ...") and give each speaker their own color, both in the Transcript panel and in the summary. Labels are generic and numbered by whoever spoke first — this doesn't identify anyone by name.

This needs a GPU. If none is detected on your machine, the checkbox is disabled with a tooltip explaining why; leave it unchecked and everything else, including summarization, works exactly as it does today. See Architecture for why this feature doesn't have a CPU fallback the way transcription itself does.

If speaker identification fails partway through for any reason, the transcript still completes normally, just without the speaker labels — you won't lose your notes over it.

docs.title: Summarizing
docs.text:
Once a transcript is ready, click ✨ Summarize. This produces structured notes with three sections:

  • Key Points — what was actually discussed
  • Decisions — anything the group agreed on
  • Action Items — who's doing what

For short meetings, this is a single request to the AI server. For long meetings, the transcript is automatically split into chunks, each summarized independently, and then combined into one final set of notes — this keeps arbitrarily long meetings from exceeding the model's context window, and means a single garbled section can't corrupt the whole summary. See Architecture for details.

You can click Summarize again at any time to regenerate the notes (for example, after switching AI server settings).

docs.title: Saving and exporting
docs.text:
• 💾 Save to chat history adds the transcript and summary to the sidebar as a new entry, titled with the date and time, so you can find it later alongside your regular chats.
  • 📤 Export .txt saves the transcript and summary as a plain text file anywhere you choose — useful for emailing to people who weren't in the room, or archiving outside the app.

docs.title: Reading the status indicators
docs.text:
• The timer shows elapsed recording time.
  • Whisper: GPU or Whisper: CPU, shown once the first transcription starts, tells you which one is doing the work. GPU is used automatically when available; this is purely informational.
  • The status text on the right of the toolbar reflects what's currently happening (Loading model..., Recording, Transcribing..., Summarizing part 2/5..., Consolidating notes 1/4... for especially long meetings, Generating final notes..., Done, or an error message if something went wrong).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Most day-to-day settings live in File → Settings, no file editing required. (Some lower-level settings are file-based — see Configuration for those.)

docs.title: AI Server Settings
docs.text:
Open File → Settings (or press Ctrl+,) to open the dialog.

Field What it does Server address The URL of your lab's Ollama server's chat endpoint, e.g. http://10.3.2.112:11434/api/chat. Change this if your lab's AI server moves to a new address. Model name The name of the model to use on that server, e.g. qwen3.6:35b-coder. Change this to switch models if your lab runs more than one.

Click Test Connection before saving to confirm the app can actually reach the server and get a response — this catches typos and network issues immediately rather than after you close the dialog.

Click Save, then restart the app for the new settings to take effect.

Why a restart?

Keeping configuration as a simple, restart-to-apply setting avoids a class of bugs where half the app is using old settings and half is using new ones mid-session — deliberately simple over deliberately clever.

docs.title: Dark mode
docs.text: View → Dark Mode switches the whole app's color theme instantly — no restart needed. Your choice is remembered for next time.

docs.title: What's not in this dialog
docs.text: The speech-to-text model size and whether it prefers GPU or CPU are set via the config.json file instead, since they're the kind of setting an administrator sets up once per machine rather than something an individual user changes day to day. See Configuration.
